scope: Eight original, multi-mark AQA-style science school-mock applications for the seven still-partial science skills. Not flashcards. Diagram and multistep marking requires actual user review.
notes: Original exam-style questions and provisional one-mark criteria, not past-paper reproductions or official schemes. Numerical answers and units independently cross-checked; every question disables automatic fuzzy marking and requires manual marks review. Practical scenarios analyse reported data only; do not instruct live experiments.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style science school-mock practical and diagram applications
questions.question: Construct and measure a non-perpendicular vector resultant
questions.subtopic: Construct and measure a non-perpendicular vector resultant
questions.prompt: Two forces act together in a horizontal plane: F₁ = 7.0 N due east; F₂ = 5.0 N at 60° north of east. On squared paper make an accurately scaled head-to-tail vector drawing and label both forces. Draw and label their resultant. Use your drawing to estimate its magnitude and direction, then check with components. Submit a photograph of the drawing for your own manual mark review. [7 marks]
markPoints: Choose an appropriate scale such as 1 cm representing 1 N and provide direction reference.
Draw a 7.0 N horizontal arrow due east to the chosen scale.
Place the 5.0 N second arrow from the FIRST HEAD, inclined 60° north of east, with correct length.
Draw resultant from the FIRST TAIL to the FINAL HEAD, with arrowhead in the correct direction.
Resolve east component Rₓ=7.0+5.0cos60°=9.5 N.
Resolve north component Rᵧ=5.0sin60°=4.33 N.
Give R≈10.4 N at ≈24.5° north of east, consistent with diagram and signs.
questions.modelAnswer: With 1 cm representing 1 N, draw 7.0 cm east. From its head draw 5.0 cm at 60° north of east. The resultant runs from the starting tail to the final head. Rₓ=7+5cos60°=9.5 N; Rᵧ=5sin60°=4.33 N. |R|=√(9.5²+4.33²)=10.44 N and θ=tan⁻¹(4.33/9.5)=24.5° north of east. The diagram must be inspected separately for scale, positioning and arrow direction.
questions.manualReviewReason: This question checks a complete diagram, graph or multi-step practical explanation. The current automatic text marker must not award marks from matching a few words; use the actual sketch or written working and adjust individual marks manually.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style science school-mock practical and diagram applications
questions.question: Free-fall g graph with error and an intercept
questions.subtopic: Free-fall g graph with error and an intercept
questions.prompt: A ball is dropped from rest. A report gives hypothetical time t / s and drop displacement s / m: (0.20, 0.20), (0.30, 0.45), (0.40, 0.80), (0.50, 1.25). Draw a graph of s against t² using these points. Give its gradient, infer g, and explain one reason a non-zero intercept or scatter may appear. Inspect the completed graph manually, not just a typed description. [7 marks]
markPoints: Calculate t² values 0.040, 0.090, 0.160 and 0.250 s².
Put t² / s² on horizontal axis and s / m on vertical axis with sensible scales.
Plot all four points in their correct locations on the s against t² graph.
Draw an appropriate straight line of best fit, rather than unconnected dot-to-dot segments.
Calculate gradient ≈(1.25−0.20)/(0.25−0.04)=5.0 m s⁻².
Use s=(1/2)gt² to find g≈2×5.0=10.0 m s⁻².
Identify an appropriate source of offset/scatter, e.g. timing zero error or variable release, and explain its effect.
questions.modelAnswer: For a body dropped from rest, s=½gt². The plotted coordinates (t²/s²,s/m) are (0.040,0.20), (0.090,0.45), (0.160,0.80), (0.250,1.25). The straight best-fit gradient is (1.25−0.20)/(0.250−0.040)=5.0 m s⁻², so g≈10.0 m s⁻². A non-zero intercept could arise from systematic displacement or timing offset, while random release/timing variation could cause scatter. The plotted axes, line and points require manual review.

questions.question: Free-fall g uncertainty and measurement limitations
questions.subtopic: Free-fall g uncertainty and measurement limitations
questions.prompt: A hypothetical free-fall experiment measures drop height h=(0.800±0.010) m and elapsed time t=(0.400±0.010) s from rest. Determine g using h=½gt². Estimate percentage uncertainty in g by adding percentage uncertainties for h and t². State one way to reduce random variation and explain why averaging cannot remove a fixed timing offset. No physical experiment is required. [7 marks]
markPoints: Rearrange to g=2h/t².
Find percentage uncertainty in h = (0.010/0.800)×100=1.25%.
Find percentage uncertainty in t = (0.010/0.400)×100=2.50%.
Double the time percentage because t is squared, to give 5.00%.
Combine percentage uncertainties 1.25%+5.00%=6.25% (first-order estimate).
Suggest repeats with an averaged result to reduce random scatter, and note a constant offset remains systematic and is not cancelled by averaging.
questions.modelAnswer: The drop starts from rest, so g=2h/t²=2×0.800/(0.400²)=10.0 m s⁻². Percentage uncertainty in h is 1.25%; in t it is 2.50%, contributing 5.00% to t². Estimated percentage uncertainty in g is 1.25%+5.00%=6.25%, i.e. roughly ±0.6 m s⁻². Repeating measurements and taking a mean can reduce random error. A fixed sensor delay or zero offset persists after averaging and must be identified or corrected separately.

questions.series: Original AQA-style science school-mock practical and diagram applications
questions.question: Explain vehicle drag, traction and aerodynamic lift
questions.subtopic: Explain vehicle drag, traction and aerodynamic lift
questions.prompt: A vehicle travels on a level straight road with forward engine/traction force 2.40 kN, aerodynamic drag 1.80 kN and other resistive forces 0.60 kN. (a) Find its net horizontal force and acceleration if mass is 1200 kg. (b) Explain why at its maximum steady speed the forward and resistive forces balance. (c) Distinguish drag, road–tyre friction/traction and aerodynamic lift, and describe how an upward lift force could alter available traction without claiming it always does. [7 marks]
markPoints: Convert total resistive forces to 1.80+0.60=2.40 kN.
Calculate net horizontal force =2.40−2.40=0 N.
Deduce acceleration a=F/m=0 m s⁻².
Explain constant-speed operation requires zero net horizontal force, not zero individual forces.
Identify drag as a fluid resistance force generally opposing relative airflow/motion.
Explain road–tyre friction can provide forward traction and depends on available contact/normal reaction.
State aerodynamic lift is perpendicular to airflow and if upward may reduce normal reaction and maximum available traction (conditions depend on vehicle design).
questions.modelAnswer: Total resistance =1.80+0.60=2.40 kN, equal to the driving/traction force. The horizontal resultant is 0 N, hence a=0/1200=0 m s⁻² and speed can remain constant. At maximum steady level-road speed, the available driving force balances resistance. Drag opposes motion relative to the air; road–tyre friction can transmit driving/traction force; aerodynamic lift acts perpendicular to relative airflow. Upward lift may reduce tyre normal reaction and therefore grip, but aerodynamic design can also create downforce.

questions.series: Original AQA-style science school-mock practical and diagram applications
questions.question: Draw and use a free-body diagram on a rough slope
questions.subtopic: Draw and use a free-body diagram on a rough slope
questions.prompt: A 2.0 kg block slides DOWN a rough plane inclined 30° to the horizontal. Friction is 3.0 N up the slope; take g=9.8 N kg⁻¹. Draw an actual labelled free-body diagram showing ONLY external forces acting on the block, and use it to calculate its acceleration down the plane. The force drawing is to be reviewed manually. [7 marks]
markPoints: Represent the block as one body with arrows for external forces only; do not draw a fictitious 'motion force'.
Draw weight W=mg=19.6 N vertically downwards.
Draw the normal reaction perpendicular OUT of the slope.
Draw friction 3.0 N parallel UP the slope, opposing sliding.
Resolve weight down the slope mg sin30°=9.8 N.
Find net down-slope force 9.8−3.0=6.8 N.
Use F=ma to obtain acceleration 6.8/2.0=3.4 m s⁻² down the slope.
questions.modelAnswer: The free-body diagram must show three and only three external forces: weight 19.6 N vertically down, normal reaction perpendicular away from the plane, and friction 3.0 N directed up the plane. The component of weight down the plane is 19.6sin30°=9.8 N, giving a net 6.8 N down the plane. Newton's second law gives a=6.8/2.0=3.4 m s⁻² down-slope. No arrow representing velocity or a separate 'resultant force' should be substituted for the actual forces.

questions.question: Interpret the full stress–strain curve of a ductile sample
questions.subtopic: Interpret the full stress–strain curve of a ductile sample
questions.prompt: A ductile metal sample initially follows a straight stress–strain line passing through (strain 0.0010, stress 150 MPa) and (strain 0.0020, stress 300 MPa). Beyond that, the curve bends, reaches a maximum stress and eventually fractures; unloading after substantial bending leaves permanent strain. Draw a labelled sketch of a plausible complete curve and use the data to find Young modulus. Identify the limit of proportionality, elastic/plastic behaviour, maximum stress and fracture. Check the sketch manually. [8 marks]
markPoints: Draw tensile stress on vertical axis and tensile strain on horizontal axis with axes labelled.
Show initial straight line from the origin, reflecting stress proportional to strain.
Mark or explain the limit of proportionality where this straight-line region ends.
Show a plausible non-linear plastic region with permanent strain on unloading.
Show a maximum/ultimate engineering stress followed by a fracture point; a ductile curve need not be a perfectly sharp peak.
Compute initial gradient Δσ/Δε=(300−150) MPa/(0.0020−0.0010)=150,000 MPa.
Convert Young modulus to E=1.50×10¹¹ Pa (150 GPa).
Explain the elastic limit is not necessarily identical to the limit of proportionality, and plastic deformation leaves a permanent extension.
questions.modelAnswer: Sketch tensile stress vertically and strain horizontally: an initial straight line through the origin, then a non-linear yielding/plastic region, a maximum engineering stress and eventual fracture. Mark that the elastic limit need not coincide with the proportional limit. Young modulus is the linear gradient: (300−150)×10⁶ Pa/(0.0020−0.0010)=1.50×10¹¹ Pa. If a plastic sample is unloaded, some strain remains. Exact drawing details should be awarded from the drawing, not by matching descriptive phrases.

questions.question: Young modulus wire data and propagated uncertainty
questions.subtopic: Young modulus wire data and propagated uncertainty
questions.prompt: A report on a wire gives original length L=1.50 m, diameter d=(0.400±0.010) mm, added force F=12.0 N and extension ΔL=(1.00±0.02) mm. Describe what must be measured for Young modulus and how a micrometer zero offset would affect the result. Calculate cross-sectional area, Young modulus and the approximate combined percentage uncertainty due ONLY to diameter and extension. This is a written data-analysis problem; no physical experiment is required. [8 marks]
markPoints: State original wire length and force/extension data are needed; measurements should be in SI units.
Identify measuring wire diameter with a micrometer at multiple positions/orientations and checking zero offset.
Convert d=4.00×10⁻⁴ m and ΔL=1.00×10⁻³ m.
Calculate area A=πd²/4≈1.26×10⁻⁷ m².
Use E=(F/A)/(ΔL/L)=FL/(AΔL).
Find E≈1.43×10¹¹ Pa.
Find % uncertainty due to d² is 2×(0.010/0.400)×100=5.0%; due to ΔL is (0.02/1.00)×100=2.0%.
Sum these contributions to ≈7.0% (excluding L and F); explain that systematic micrometer zero error biases all diameter/area results and cannot be removed by averaging.
questions.modelAnswer: Take original length and extension measurements, force and representative diameter; check a micrometer for a constant zero offset and take repeated diameters at different points/orientations. d=0.000400 m, extension=0.00100 m. A=πd²/4=1.2566×10⁻⁷ m². E=12.0×1.50/(A×0.00100)=1.43×10¹¹ Pa. For diameter, 2×(0.010/0.400)×100=5.0%; for extension, (0.02/1.00)×100=2.0%; first-order combined percentage uncertainty is about 7.0%, excluding F and L. Micrometer zero error is systematic, not removed by a mean.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style science school-mock practical and diagram applications
questions.question: Calorimetry heat-loss evaluation with uncertainty
questions.prompt: A report describes a hypothetical exothermic reaction heating 100.0 g of solution by ΔT=(6.0±0.2) °C; c=4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and 0.0500 mol of reactant is consumed. Calculate q and molar ΔH. Explain the purpose of an insulated cup, lid and mixing, why a temperature–time extrapolation may improve the estimate, and how heat lost to surroundings affects the calculated ΔH. State the percentage uncertainty arising from ΔT alone. No experiment or chemicals are required. [8 marks]
markPoints: Use q=mcΔT with solution mass 100.0 g, c=4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and ΔT=6.0 K.
Calculate heat gained by solution q=100.0×4.18×6.0=2508 J (2.508 kJ).
Use reaction sign: heat released by system is negative when solution warms.
Explain cup insulation and lid reduce heat exchange with surroundings; stirring promotes a representative uniform temperature.
Explain extrapolating the temperature–time trend back to mixing helps correct heat lost/gained during measurement.
State heat lost to surroundings would underestimate measured rise and yield ΔH that is not negative enough (underestimated magnitude).
Calculate percentage uncertainty due to ΔT alone =0.2/6.0×100≈3.33%.
questions.modelAnswer: The heat gained by the solution is q=100.0×4.18×6.0=2508 J=2.508 kJ. Since the reaction is exothermic, ΔH=−2.508/0.0500=−50.16≈−50.2 kJ mol⁻¹. An insulated cup and lid limit unwanted heat transfer, while stirring makes the recorded temperature more representative. Temperature–time extrapolation towards mixing can improve the estimated peak rise. Heat lost to the room makes measured q too small, so ΔH is less negative than the true value. The percentage uncertainty due to ΔT alone is 0.2/6.0×100=3.33%.
